lines: Only 5 legal anchors exist (e_r1…e_r5, all right edge, 6% escape, battery in the near field), so the first batch spans all five with IFAs at λ/4-ish lengths plus gap/height variation to find which anchor has the most usable impedance.

c002 (e_r2, IFA, 30.7 mm, gap 5 mm) is far ahead: S11 −15.9 dB, VSWR 1.38, 97% efficiency, resonance only 20 MHz high. Gap 5 mm is the right feed tap (8 mm → R≈120–160 Ω, 3 mm → R≈10 Ω). Sweeping length to centre the band.

lines: Length is nailed: 30.75–31.0 mm puts resonance at 2.46 GHz with VSWR 1.37 and 97.5% efficiency. Remaining knob is the residual +16 Ω inductive reactance, so I'm co-varying gap and arm height around that optimum before concluding.

action.rationale: Only 5 anchors are legal (e_r1..e_r5, right edge); all others intersect real metal. All five have identical 6% escape fraction, so selection came down to impedance behaviour: e_r2 gave the best-behaved feed, with e_r1 (speaker-loaded, R collapses to 19 ohm) and e_r3 (resonance 5% high, R=29 ohm) both markedly worse. Length sweep 29-33 mm fixed the resonance: 30.75 mm resonates at 2.4609 GHz with worst in-band S11 of -8 dB or better across 2.4-2.4835 GHz, VSWR 1.37, 97.5% total efficiency. Gap 5 mm is the correct feed tap: 3 mm drops R to ~10 ohm and 8 mm pushes it to 120-160 ohm, both failing VSWR. c019 (31.0 mm / 5.5 mm gap) is the runner-up with the deepest usable notch (-20.3 dB) and slightly wider bandwidth but R=63 ohm; c016 (2.5 mm height) trades 1.7 dB of match for 19 MHz more bandwidth as a tolerance hedge. Caveat: no legal anchor meets the 12 mm metal keep-out - the battery pack is 0.2 mm from the radiator - so the simulated 97.5% efficiency assumes the battery geometry as given; production tuning must be done in-situ, and a mechanical change (battery inset on the right edge, or a segmented frame band freeing a bottom corner) is the real fix.

lines: Plateaued — c013 is the design: e_r2 IFA, 30.75 mm, 5 mm feed-short gap, 2 mm height. In-band S11 ≤ −8 dB across 2.4–2.4835 GHz (−16.1 dB at resonance), VSWR 1.37, Z = 49+j16 Ω, 97.5% efficiency, 173 MHz of −6 dB bandwidth. Every one of the 5 legal anchors violates the 12 mm keep-out (battery cell sits 0.2 mm away) — that is a mechanical constraint, not something tuning can fix: the battery would have to shrink ~12 mm on the right edge, or the frame band be segmented at a corner, to clear it.

final.rationale: Only 5 of 20 anchors are legal (e_r1..e_r5, all right edge, 6% escape fraction); the rest intersect real metal. Selection came down to impedance behaviour: e_r2 gave the best-behaved feed, e_r1 is speaker-loaded (R collapses to 19 ohm) and e_r3 resonates 5% high with R=29 ohm. A 29-33 mm length sweep fixed resonance at 30.75 mm -> 2.4609 GHz, worst in-band S11 <= -8 dB over 2.4-2.4835 GHz (-16.1 dB at resonance), Z = 48.9 + j15.7 ohm, VSWR 1.37, total efficiency 0.975, 172.6 MHz of -6 dB bandwidth. Gap 5 mm is the correct feed tap (3 mm -> R~10 ohm, 8 mm -> R 120-160 ohm, both fail VSWR). Runner-up c019 (31.0 mm / 5.5 mm gap) has the deepest notch (-20.3 dB) and 191.7 MHz bandwidth but R=63 ohm; c016 (2.5 mm height) trades 1.7 dB of match for extra bandwidth as a tolerance hedge. Caveat: no legal anchor meets the 12 mm metal keep-out - the battery pack sits 0.2 mm from the radiator - so simulated efficiency assumes the battery geometry as given; the real fix is mechanical (battery inset on the right edge, or a segmented frame band freeing a bottom corner).
